title: A Pound of Flour
body:
A Pound of Flour

To establish his sovereignty and purify the land, Emperor Yudhishthira celebrated the grand Aswamedha Yajna (Horse Sacrifice) at Hastinapur. It was an exhibition of unprecedented wealth; millions of Brahmanas, kings, and poor people gathered from all corners of the earth, receiving bounteous gifts of gold, cattle, and grain. Everything was completed in perfect, flawless conformity with scriptural injunctions, and Yudhishthira felt a quiet pride in his heart.
Suddenly, right in the middle of the sacrificial pavilion, a strange weasel appeared. Half of its body was made of shining, pure gold. Rolling on the ground, the weasel laughed with a loud, human laugh of derision: 'Princes assembled and priests, listen to me! You believe you have completed a grand sacrifice. But your horse sacrifice and all your showy gifts are less than the simple gift of a pound of maize flour made by a poor Brahmana family here in Kurukshetra.'
The proud assembly was stunned. The chief priests, highly offended, demanded an explanation. The weasel turned its golden eye upon them and narrated the story of the poor Brahmana family who lived under the strict Unchhavritti discipline (eating only scattered grains gleaned from the fields after harvest):
During a terrible famine, the Brahmana, his wife, his son, and his daughter-in-law had fasted for days. One afternoon, they managed to glean a small handful of maize, which they ground into a single pound of flour, dividing it into four equal shares for their only meal of the day.
Just as they sat down to eat, a hungry traveler appeared at their door. Without hesitation, the father gave his share of the flour to the guest. The guest ate it but remained hungry. Then, the wife stepped forward, offering her share. The father protested, but the wife insisted: 'Dharma and all objects of human activity are to our common benefit. Take my share and satisfy the guest.' The guest ate it but was still hungry. The son then offered his share, declaring: 'It is the duty of the son to protect his father and serve the guest. My share is yours.' Finally, the daughter-in-law surrendered her share as well, despite her extreme emaciation, saying: 'My body is dedicated to the service of this household. Let this guest be satisfied.'
The guest, who was Lord Dharma in disguise, was highly pleased. He threw off his disguise, showered flowers upon the household, and took all four of them in a divine chariot directly to Vaikuntham, praising their sacrifice. The weasel concluded: 'I was nearby and caught the fragrance of that sacred flour. It turned one side of my body into pure gold. I have traveled to every grand yajna in the world since then, hoping to turn my other side into gold, but no sacrifice—not even this lavish horse sacrifice of Yudhishthira—can match the purity, love, and absolute selflessness of that poor Brahmana's pound of flour. Your yajna is a product of wealth and pride; theirs was a product of pure devotion.' Saying this, the weasel vanished, leaving Yudhishthira's pride completely shattered.
